chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Majilawayh narrated to me from his uncle Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abu Ayyub, from Abu Hamza al-Thumali, who said:

A man said to Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him), 'You have left Jihad and its difficulty, and have adhered to Hajj and its ease.' He said, 'And he was leaning (back), so he sat up and said, 'Woe to you! Did not reach you what the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said during his Farewell Pilgrimage?'

Indeed, when the sun was about to set, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said, 'O Bilal, tell the people to be silent.' And when they were silent, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said, 'Indeed, your Lord has been gracious to you on this day; He has forgiven your righteous ones and accepted the intercession of your righteous ones for your sinners, so go forth, forgiven for you, and He has guaranteed for those with obligations from Him, His pleasure.'
ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (a.s.) defend his choice of Hajj over Jihad?
ai.summary: Imam Zayn al-Abidin (a.s.) elevates Hajj from a mere ritual to a spiritual equivalent of Jihad by citing the Prophet’s Farewell Sermon, which declares that on this day, God’s mercy has forgiven the righteous and allowed their intercession to secure forgiveness for the sinners. This narration, found in Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Thawab al-A’mal*, underscores the Shia scholarly view that the spiritual purification and divine acceptance attained through Hajj carry the weight of striving in the path of God, effectively balancing the physical exertion of Jihad with the devotional intensity of pilgrimage.
